If you feel like you can’t fall asleep at night, try turning off electronics before bedtime or turn on your computer while you’re awake.

During the winter, take breaks when possible, but avoid using devices in bed as they may interfere with our bodies’ ability to relax. Try to stay away from electronic devices until you get up to work and eat breakfast. Make sure you are not too close to bedtime by keeping your bedroom cool, darken your bedroom, and stay in the shade.
3. Exercise regularly.
Exercise has been shown to help people lose weight, lower blood pressure, and improve mood. The National Institute of Health recommends exercising five to seven times each week. However, if you must exercise, make sure to consult your physician before beginning any new activity.

Kowalski takes a few hours to observe and learn about the animals that live in coral reefs.
In the 1960s, she discovered that there were more than 250 million individual corals in the world, and that one-third of the corals found are endemic. Over the course of time, they have become so numerous that their numbers have doubled or tripled over the last century. Now, thanks to scientists from around the globe, Kowalski has uncovered a new population of 375 species.
“We knew it was going on,” says Kowalski, who is also a marine biologist with the Smithsonian Marine Science Institute. “Now we’re finding more corals.”
Kowalski first noticed them at one time during a large recent visit to Florida in 1974. She described them as small, about 2.5 inches (7 centimeters) long. They had a tiny head, no teeth, and a prominent neck. The mouth of the sea is like a snorkel for fish and can hold up to 100 pounds of prey.
